title: Top Tokens by Frequency
description: Count word frequencies and return the k most common tokens without importing Counter.

explanation.overview: Interviewers often ask you to tally frequencies, then pick a top-k list with a stable tie-break.

keyTerms.definition: A dict mapping tokens to counts in average O(1) time per update.
Sorting by (-count, word) ranks high counts first and ties alphabetically.

explanation.howItWorks:
1. Split and lowercase the text.
2. Increment a dict of counts.
3. Sort pairs by descending count, then name.
4. Slice the first k names.
explanation.designPattern: Count then rank: build a map, then sort the items.

quiz.question: What does counts.get(token, 0) return for a new token?
quiz.explanation: get returns the default 0 when the key is missing.

quiz.question: Why is the sort key (-item[1], item[0])?
options: It sorts by length then count
It ranks high counts first and breaks ties alphabetically
quiz.explanation: Negating the count sorts descending; the word is the tie-breaker.

quiz.question: After the loop, what is counts['to'] for the sample call?
quiz.explanation: The sample text has two occurrences of 'to'.

title: Pair Sum in a Sorted List
description: Find two indices whose values add to a target in a sorted list using two pointers.

explanation.overview: On a sorted array, two pointers close in from both ends in linear time.

keyTerms.definition: A pair of indices that move according to a comparison instead of nested loops.
Because the list is sorted, moving left increases the sum and moving right decreases it.

explanation.howItWorks: Compare the end-pair sum to the target. Walk the left pointer up when the sum is small, the right pointer down when it is large.
explanation.designPattern: Two pointers on a sorted sequence.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of this scan?
quiz.explanation: Each pointer moves at most n times.

quiz.question: If the current sum is too small, which pointer moves?
quiz.explanation: A larger left value increases the sum on a sorted list.

quiz.question: What does pair_sum([2, 3, 6, 9], 9) return?
quiz.explanation: 3 + 6 = 9 at indices 1 and 2.

title: Balanced Delimiters
description: Check that brackets, braces, and parentheses nest correctly using a stack.

explanation.overview: Matching delimiters is the classic stack interview problem: last opened must close first.

keyTerms.definition: Last-in, first-out structure — here a Python list with append/pop.
The most recently opened opener must match the next closer.

explanation.howItWorks: Push openers. On a closer, pop if it matches; otherwise fail. The stack must be empty at the end.

quiz.question: What does stack[-1] read?
quiz.explanation: The end of the list is the top of the stack.

quiz.question: Why return not stack at the end?
options: Unmatched openers mean the text is not balanced
quiz.explanation: Leftover openers were never closed.

quiz.question: What does balanced('{[()]}') return?
quiz.explanation: Each closer matches the most recent opener.

title: Binary Search Index
description: Return the index of a target in a sorted list, or -1, using binary search.

explanation.overview: Binary search halves the remaining range each step on a sorted list.

keyTerms.definition: The middle index of the current inclusive range.
lo and hi both still contain candidate indices.

explanation.howItWorks: Compare nums[mid] to the target and discard the half that cannot contain it.

quiz.question: Why must the list be sorted?
options: Discarding a half is only safe when order is known
quiz.explanation: The comparison tells you which side can hold the target only if values increase.

quiz.question: What is the usual time complexity?
quiz.explanation: The range halves each iteration.

quiz.question: What does index_of([1, 4, 9, 16, 25], 16) return?
quiz.explanation: 16 sits at index 3.

title: Maximum Window Sum
description: Find the maximum sum of any contiguous window of length k.

explanation.overview: A sliding window updates the sum in O(1) by adding the entering value and subtracting the leaving one.

keyTerms.definition: A subarray of fixed length that advances one index at a time.
The current window total, maintained instead of rescoring from scratch.

explanation.howItWorks: Seed with the first k items, then slide: add nums[i], drop nums[i-k], track the max.

quiz.question: What does nums[i] - nums[i - k] represent?
options: The value entering minus the value leaving the window
quiz.explanation: That difference updates the window sum in constant time.

quiz.question: Why return None when k > len(nums)?
options: No window of that length exists
quiz.explanation: You cannot form a contiguous block longer than the list.

quiz.question: What is max_window([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3)?
quiz.explanation: Windows: 8, 7, 9, 6 — the max is 9.

title: Best Subarray Sum
description: Find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray (Kadane’s algorithm).

explanation.overview: At each index you either start a new subarray or extend the previous one.

keyTerms.definition: Linear scan that tracks the best ending-here sum and the global best.
If value alone beats value plus the previous run, start over.

explanation.howItWorks: current is the best sum ending at this index. best is the max of those.

quiz.question: What does max(value, current + value) decide?
options: Whether to start a new subarray or extend
quiz.explanation: If the previous run hurts, drop it and start at value.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity?
quiz.explanation: One pass over the list.

title: Merge Overlapping Ranges
description: Merge overlapping [start, end] intervals after sorting by start.

explanation.overview: Sort intervals, then extend the last merged range when the next one overlaps.

keyTerms.definition: The next start is not after the current end.
Process intervals in order of start time.

explanation.howItWorks: Sort, seed merged with the first range, and either extend last[1] or append a new range.

quiz.question: Why sort first?
options: So overlaps are adjacent in the scan
quiz.explanation: Once starts are ordered, you only compare with the last merged interval.

quiz.question: When do we extend last[1]?
quiz.explanation: That is the overlap (or touch) condition used here.

quiz.question: What does merge_ranges([[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10]]) return?
quiz.explanation: [1,3] overlaps [2,6] into [1,6]; [8,10] stays separate.

title: Tiny LRU Cache
description: Implement get/put with insertion-ordered dict as a least-recently-used cache.

explanation.overview: Python dicts remember insertion order, so the first key is the least recently used after you move hits to the end.

keyTerms.definition: Evict the item that has gone unused the longest.
pop then re-insert so the key becomes most recent.

explanation.howItWorks: get restamps a key. put restamps or, if at capacity, drops next(iter(data)).

quiz.question: What does next(iter(self.data)) yield?
quiz.explanation: Iteration order is insertion order; the first key is least recent.

quiz.question: Why pop before re-inserting on get?
options: To move the key to the most-recent end
quiz.explanation: Re-inserting appends, marking the key as recently used.

quiz.question: After put a, put b, get a, which key is oldest?
quiz.explanation: get('a') restamped a, so b is now least recent.

title: Connected Groups
description: Count connected groups in an undirected graph with depth-first search.

explanation.overview: Each DFS walk from an unseen node discovers one connected component.

keyTerms.definition: A maximal set of nodes reachable from each other.
Prevents revisiting nodes and infinite loops on cycles.

explanation.howItWorks: For every node, if unseen, walk its edges recursively and increment the group count.

quiz.question: Why keep a seen set?
options: To avoid cycling forever on undirected links
quiz.explanation: a-b-a would recurse forever without it.

quiz.question: When does count increase?
options: Each time we start a walk from an unseen node
quiz.explanation: One increment per new component.

quiz.question: What does groups({'a': ['b'], 'b': ['a'], 'c': []}) return?
quiz.explanation: a-b is one group; c is another.

title: Shortest Hops
description: Find the fewest hops between two nodes in an unweighted graph using BFS.

explanation.overview: On unweighted edges, the first time BFS reaches a node is the shortest hop count.

keyTerms.definition: Explore neighbors in layers using a queue.
A double-ended queue with O(1) popleft.

explanation.howItWorks: Queue pairs of (node, distance). Mark seen when enqueued so each node is processed once.
explanation.designPattern: Breadth-first search for shortest path in hops.

quiz.question: Why use popleft instead of pop?
options: To process oldest nodes first (a queue)
quiz.explanation: BFS needs FIFO order.

quiz.question: Why add to seen when enqueuing, not when dequeuing?
quiz.explanation: Otherwise the same neighbor could be queued many times.

quiz.question: What does the sample hops call return?
quiz.explanation: a to d is two hops via b or c.

title: Streaming Top Scores
description: Track the k highest scores in a stream with a min-heap.

explanation.overview: A min-heap of size k stores the current champions; the root is the smallest of the best.

keyTerms.definition: A tree where the smallest value sits at index 0.
Pop the root and push a new value in one step.

explanation.howItWorks: Fill the heap to k. Then replace the root whenever a new score beats it. Sort descending to report.

quiz.question: What does heap[0] represent here?
options: The smallest of the current top k
quiz.explanation: A min-heap root is the minimum stored value.

quiz.question: When do we heapreplace?
options: When the heap is full and score > heap[0]
quiz.explanation: Only a value better than the current weakest champion belongs in the heap.

quiz.question: What does top_k([4, 9, 1, 7, 8, 2], 3) return?
quiz.explanation: The three highest scores are 9, 8, and 7.

title: Lazy Pipeline
description: Chain generators to filter and transform a stream without building extra lists.

explanation.overview: Generators pull values only when the next consumer asks, so the pipeline stays lazy.

keyTerms.definition: Pauses the function and hands one value to the caller.
Work happens on demand, not up front.

explanation.howItWorks: take pulls from squared, which pulls from evens, which pulls from range — three items only.

quiz.question: How many even numbers does take(3, ...) request?
quiz.explanation: take stops after three yielded values.

quiz.question: What does yield do inside evens?
options: Produces the next even number and pauses
quiz.explanation: yield turns the function into a generator.

quiz.question: What is list(take(3, squared(evens(range(20)))))?
quiz.explanation: Evens 0, 2, 4 squared are 0, 4, 16.

title: Timing Decorator
description: Write a decorator that records how long a function ran using a closure.

explanation.overview: Decorators wrap a function and return a new callable that can add timing, caching, or auth.

keyTerms.definition: wrapper remembers fn from the enclosing timed() call.
Copies name and docstring from the original function.

explanation.howItWorks: timed returns wrapper. Each call timestamps perf_counter around fn and stores last_elapsed on wrapper.

quiz.question: What does @timed on add mean?
quiz.explanation: The decorator syntax rebinds the name to the wrapper.

quiz.question: Why use wraps(fn)?
quiz.explanation: Otherwise the wrapper would expose the name 'wrapper'.

quiz.question: Where is last_elapsed stored?
quiz.explanation: The wrapper object holds the most recent duration.

title: Context Manager
description: Implement a context manager that tracks whether a block succeeded.

explanation.overview: __enter__/__exit__ power the with statement. __exit__ receives exception info if the block failed.

keyTerms.definition: The exception class, or None if the block finished cleanly.
Do not swallow the exception; let it propagate.

explanation.howItWorks: with calls __enter__, runs the block, then __exit__. ok is True only when exc_type is None.

quiz.question: When is t.ok True?
options: When the with block raised nothing
quiz.explanation: ok is set from exc_type is None.

quiz.question: What does returning False from __exit__ mean?
quiz.explanation: A true return value would swallow the error.

quiz.question: What does the sample print?
quiz.explanation: 1 + 1 does not raise, so ok is True.

title: Task Order
description: Produce a valid order of tasks given prerequisites using Kahn’s algorithm.

explanation.overview: Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly takes nodes with indegree 0. If you cannot finish, there is a cycle.

keyTerms.definition: How many prerequisites still point at a node.
An order where every edge goes from earlier to later.

explanation.howItWorks: Count incoming edges, queue zeros, emit a node, decrement neighbors, repeat.

quiz.question: What does incoming[dst] += 1 record?
options: That dst has one more prerequisite
quiz.explanation: Each edge is one incoming dependency on dst.

quiz.question: Why return None if len(order) != len(nodes)?
options: A cycle (or missing node) blocked the sort
quiz.explanation: Leftover nodes still had indegree > 0.

quiz.question: What does the sample print?
quiz.explanation: a before b before c satisfies both edges.

title: Disjoint Sets
description: Union-find with path compression to test whether two people share a group.

explanation.overview: Union-find tracks components. find walks to the root; path compression flattens the tree.

keyTerms.definition: Each node points toward its group representative.
After find, point the node straight at the root.

explanation.howItWorks: union links two roots. same is true when both names share a root after find.

quiz.question: What does find do when parent[name] != name?
options: Recurses to the root and compresses the path
quiz.explanation: That assignment is path compression.

quiz.question: When does union skip linking?
options: When a and b already share a root
quiz.explanation: If ra == rb they are already in one group.

quiz.question: What does the sample print?
quiz.explanation: ann and bea were united; cam was not.
